The authors argue that they therefore tried their utmost not only to appeal their original convictions and sentences as is set out in their complaints to the Committee, but also to have another court adjudicate the violations of their rights as set out in the Constitution, to no avail.Lack of cooperation by the State Party 7.On 2 July 2018 (communication No. 3167/2018) and 19 March 2020 (communication No. 3218/2018) the State Party was informed that its request for the admissibility of the communications to be examined separately from the merits had been denied and it was requested to submit its observations on the merits of the communications. Reminders to the State Party to submit the observations on the merits were sent on 28 August 2019 (communication No. 3167/2018), 24 November 2021 (communication Nos. 3167/2018 and 3218/2018) and 30 January 2025 (communication Nos. 3167/2018 and 3218/2018). The Committee regrets the failure of the State Party to respond to these requests in a timely manner and to provide any information with regard to the merits of the authors’ claims. The Committee recalls that article 4 (2) of the Optional Protocol implicitly obliges States Parties to examine in good faith all allegations brought against them and to make available to the Committee all the information at their disposal. In the absence of a reply from the State Party, due weight must be given to the authors’ allegations, to the extent that they are substantiated.Issues and proceedings before the CommitteeConsideration of admissibility8.1Before considering any claims contained in a communication, the Committee must decide, in accordance with rule 97 of its rules of procedure, whether the communication is admissible under the Optional Protocol.8.2The Committee has ascertained, as required under article 5 (2) (a) of the Optional Protocol, that the same matter is not being examined under another procedure of international investigation or settlement. 8.3The Committee notes the State Party’s submission that the communications should be found inadmissible under article 5 (2) (b) of the Optional Protocol for failure to exhaust domestic remedies. It notes the authors’ argument that after their convictions they submitted applications for leave to appeal before the trial court as stipulated under domestic law, and that following the rejection of said applications, they submitted petitions before the Supreme Court of Appeal. It further notes their argument that considering the lengthy trial, the proceedings in their case have also been unduly prolonged.8.4The Committee recalls its jurisprudence that, although there is no obligation to exhaust domestic remedies if they have no chance of being successful or if the application of remedies is unreasonably prolonged, authors of communications must exercise due diligence in the pursuit of available remedies, and that mere doubts or assumptions about their effectiveness do not absolve the authors from exhausting them. 8.5In the present case the Committee notes that following their conviction and sentencing all three authors made applications for leave to appeal to the trial court, which rejected their applications on 30 January 2014 (communication No. 3167/2018) and 26 September 2016 (communication No. 3218/2018). The Committee notes the State Party’s argument that the applications for leave to appeal by Johan and Wilhelm Pretorius was filed over two years after their sentencing, thus failing to meet the deadline of filing an application for leave to appeal within 14 days of the judgment as stipulated in the Criminal Procedure Act. The Committee however notes the authors’ undisputed argument that the trial court excused the late filing of the application. The Committee further notes that following the rejection by the trial court of their applications for leave to appeal, all three authors submitted petitions to the Supreme Court of Appeal containing their claims of fair trial violations (see paras. 2.8-2.9). The Committee notes the authors’ information that the Registrar of the Supreme Court of Appeal refused to accept the petition by Johan Lets Pretorius on the ground that the trial judgement on conviction and sentence, the leave to appeal judgement and the trial record were not attached to the petition and their information that the Registrar refused the petition by Johan and Wilhelm Pretorius as it did not contain the judgement on conviction and sentence of the trial court. The Committee further notes the authors’ unrefuted argument that it was not possible to submit said documents together with their petition, as at the time of the submission of the petitions before the Supreme Court of Appeal they had not received the documentation from the trial court, and that in the case of Johan Pretorius and Wilhelm Pretorius who were unrepresented, it was additionally not a requirement under domestic law to submit said documents together with the petition. 8.6The Committee further notes the State Party’s submission that the authors could also have filed claims before the Constitutional Court. It notes the authors’ argument that their request to be appointed a legal aid lawyer for filing such a petition was denied on 28 March 2018 and their argument that the infringements of their rights had already occurred in view of the excessively long trial. The Committee further notes that the State Party has not provided any further information on the possibility in the authors case to obtain a remedy from the Constitutional Court to address their claims, following the rejection of their applications for leave to appeal. Taking into account the authors’ information on the attempts made to exhaust domestic remedies by submitting applications for leave to appeal before the trial court and by filing petitions before the Supreme Court of Appeal, as well as taking into account the fact, that by the time the authors’ petitions before the Supreme Court of Appeal were rejected in 2016 and 2017, 13 years had elapsed since their arrest, the Committee considers that it is not precluded by article 5 (2) (b) of the Optional Protocol from considering the present communication.8.7The Committee notes the authors’ claim that their rights under article 9 (1) and 14 (1-2) of the Covenant were violated as they were transported to the court hearings in arm-and-foot chains, and as photos of them in chains were published in media, thus presenting them as dangerous criminals. It further notes their claims that the excessively long trial also violated the presumption of innocence under article 14 (2), as considering their long periods of detention they were prejudged as being guilty. The Committee also notes the authors’ claims that the selection of defendants and state witnesses was done arbitrarily in violation of their rights under articles 9 (1), 14 (1) and 26. The Committee further notes the authors’ claims that the trial court in sentencing them failed to take into account the principles of reformation and rehabilitation in violation of their rights under article 10 (3) of the Covenant. The Committee however considers that the authors have not sufficiently substantiated these claims, and it therefore finds the claims inadmissible under article 2 of the Optional Protocol.8.8The Committee notes the authors’ claims that the fact that they had to attend court sessions regularly or the fact that they were detained throughout the trial violated their right to liberty and security of person under article 9 (1), as well as their claim that their rights under article 12 (1-2) were violated as they could not travel freely or choose their place of residence during the trial. In the absence of any further specific information or argumentation as to said claims, the Committee finds the claims to be insufficiently substantiated for the purposes of admissibility and inadmissible under article 2 of the Optional Protocol.8.9The Committee further notes the authors’ claims that their rights under articles 9 (1) and 14 (1) were violated as the trial court’s composition was not based in law and as the trial judge and one of the assessors in the hearing were former colleagues of the senior advocate of the prosecuting team. The Committee however notes that the authors have not provided any further specific information or argumentation in support of these claims, and it therefore finds the claims to be insufficiently substantiated for the purposes of admissibility and inadmissible under article 2 of the Optional Protocol.8.10The Committee however considers that the authors have sufficiently substantiated the remaining claims on: their right to be present at trial; their lack of legal representation; the undue delay in proceedings; the right to review; and the right to confidential communication with counsel, for the purposes of admissibility. Accordingly, the Committee declares the authors’ claims under articles 14 (3) (b), (c), (d), 14 (5) and 17 of the Covenant admissible and proceeds with its consideration of the merits.Consideration of the merits 9.1The Committee has considered the communication in the light of all the information submitted to it by the parties, in accordance with article 5 (1) of the Optional Protocol. The Committee notes that, in failing to respond to a communication, or responding incompletely, a State that is the object of a communication puts itself at a disadvantage because the Committee is then compelled to consider the communication in the absence of full information relating to the communication. In the absence of any explanations from the State Party in respect of the merits, due weight must be given to the author’s allegations to the extent that they have been sufficiently substantiated (see para. 7 above).9.2The Committee notes the authors’ claims that their rights under article 14 (3) (d) of the Covenant were violated as they were not present during parts of the trial, were unrepresented during periods of the trial, and were not appointed counsel representing them individually. The Committee recalls that article 14 (3) (d) guarantees the right of the accused person to be tried in his or her presence and to have legal assistance assigned to him or her whenever the interests of justice so require, and without payment by them in any such case if they do not have sufficient means for such payment. The Committee further recalls that the gravity of the offence is important in deciding whether counsel should be assigned “in the interest of justice” as is the existence of some objective chance of success at the appeals stage. 9.3In the present case, concerning the gravity of the offences in question, the Committee notes that the authors were on trial for serious criminal charges, facing long periods of imprisonment if convicted. The Committee notes the authors’ claims that they were not present at parts of the trial, including testimonies by key witnesses. It further notes their claims that they were unrepresented for periods of five months (communication No. 3167/2018) and one year and seven months (communication No. 3218/2018), including during testimonies of witnesses upon which their convictions were based. The Committee finally notes their claims that counsel eventually appointed for them through the Legal Aid Board also represented other defendants in the case without the Board having assessed whether there was a conflict of interest amongst the defendants (see paras. 3.8-3.10). The Committee notes that the State Party has not submitted any observations on the merits of the present communication or refuted any of the authors’ claims. In the absence of a response from the State Party in that regard, the Committee gives due weight to the authors’ claims that they were not present at parts of the trial, were unrepresented during crucial periods of the trial, and that there was no assessment made as to whether there was a conflict of interest among defendants represented by the same counsel appointed to them, thus amounting to a violation of the authors’ rights under article 14 (3) (d) of the Covenant.9.4The Committee notes the authors’ claim that their right under article 14 (3) (c) to be tried without undue delay was violated, as by the time they were sentenced at first instance in October 2013, 11 years had passed since their arrests in September and December 2002. The Committee recalls that the right of the accused to be tried without undue delay is not only designed to avoid keeping persons too long in a state of uncertainty about their fate and, if held in detention during the period of the trial, to ensure that such deprivation of liberty does not last longer than necessary in the circumstances of the specific case, but also to serve the interests of justice. What is reasonable has to be assessed in the circumstances of each case, taking into account mainly the complexity of the case, the conduct of the accused, and the manner in which the matter was dealt with by the administrative and judicial authorities. In cases where the accused are denied bail by the court, they must be tried as expeditiously as possible. The Committee further recalls that this guarantee relates not only to the time between the formal charging of the accused and the time by which a trial should commence, but also the time until the final judgement on appeal. All stages, whether in first instance or on appeal must take place without undue delay.9.5In the present case the Committee notes the authors’ argument that their trial at first instance lasted 11 years, with two of the authors detained during this period. It notes the State Party’s argument that parts of the delays were attributable to the defendants’ requests for postponements of hearing sessions, including postponement requests made by the authors. The Committee however notes the authors’ argument that the State Party has not provided any example of any alleged requests for postponement made by them that it considered to be without merit. It further notes their arguments that the trial was delayed as accused were joined to the same trial despite counsels’ objection that this would unduly prolong the trial and their argument that the delays were partly caused by delays by the Legal Aid Board in appointing legal representatives for some of the defendants. In the absence of any further explanation by the State Party regarding the excessive length of the trial, the Committee gives due weight to the authors’ claims and finds that the facts described, amount to a violation of their rights under article 14 (3) (c) of the Covenant.9.6The Committee further notes the authors’ claim that their rights under article 14 (5) of the Covenant were violated as they were unable to have their convictions and sentences reviewed by a higher tribunal. The Committee recalls that the right to have one’s conviction and sentence reviewed by a higher tribunal imposes on the State Party a duty to review substantively, both on the basis of sufficiency of the evidence and of the law, the conviction and sentence, such that the procedure allows for due consideration of the nature of the case. A review that is limited to the formal or legal aspects of the conviction without any consideration whatsoever of the facts is not sufficient under the Covenant. The Committee further recalls that the right to have one’s conviction reviewed can only be exercised effectively if the convicted person is entitled to have access to a duly reasoned, written judgement of the trial court, and, at least in the court of first appeal where domestic law provides for several instances of appeal, also to other documents, such as trial transcripts, necessary to enjoy the effective exercise of the right to appeal.9.7In the present case, the Committee notes the authors’ argument that at the time of the submission of their complaint before the Committee over 15 years had passed since their arrest and detention without them having been able to have their convictions and sentences reviewed by a higher tribunal. It notes their information that after their applications for leave to appeal before the trial court had been rejected, they submitted petitions to the Supreme Court of Appeal which were refused on the ground that documentation such as the trial judgement on conviction and sentence, the leave to appeal judgement and the trial record were not attached to the petition. The Committee further notes the authors’ argument that it was not possible for them to submit said documents, as at the time of the submission of the petitions before the Supreme Court of Appeal they had not received the requested documentation. The Committee thus notes the authors’ submission that despite attempts to have their conviction and sentence reviewed by a higher tribunal, their appeals were rejected without any consideration of the facts in their case or review of the claims raised by them concerning fair trial violations. In the absence of any explanation by the State Party in this regard, the Committee gives due weight to the authors’ claims and finds that the facts described, amount to a violation of their rights under article 14 (5) of the Covenant.9.8The Committee further notes the authors’ claims that their conversations with their legal representatives were monitored with both audio and visual surveillance during the court proceedings. The Committee recalls that the right to communicate with counsel requires that counsel should be able to meet their clients in private and to communicate with the accused in conditions that fully respect the confidentiality of their communications. In the present case the Committee notes the authors’ claims that the court microphone system recorded consultations between defendants and counsel which took place in court, that their cells, where consultations between legal representatives and defendants sometimes occurred were monitored, as well as their claim that the consultation rooms in the court building were monitored. In the absence of any submission by the State Party refuting the authors’ claims in this regard, the Committee gives due weight to the authors’ claims and finds that the facts described, amount to a violation of their rights under article 14 (3) (b) of the Covenant. Having thus concluded, the Committee will not separately consider the same claims raised by the authors under article 17 of the Covenant.10. The Committee, acting under article 5 (4) of the Optional Protocol, is of the view that the facts before it disclose a violation of the authors’ rights under articles 14 (3) (b), (c) and (d) and 14 (5) of the Covenant. 11. Pursuant to article 2 (3) (a) of the Covenant, the State Party is under an obligation to provide the authors with an effective remedy. This requires it to make full reparation to individuals whose Covenant rights have been violated. The Committee considers that, in the present case, its Views on the merits of the complaint constitute sufficient reparation for the violations found. The State Party is also under an obligation to take steps to prevent similar violations occurring in the future. 12. Bearing in mind that, by becoming a party to the Optional Protocol, the State Party has recognized the competence of the Committee to determine whether there has been a violation of the Covenant and that, pursuant to article 2 of the Covenant, the State Party has undertaken to ensure to all individuals within its territory and subject to its jurisdiction the rights recognized in the Covenant and to provide an effective remedy when it has been determined that a violation has occurred, the Committee wishes to receive from the State Party, within 180 days, information about the measures taken to give effect to the Committee’s Views. The State Party is also requested to publish the present Views and to have them widely disseminated in the languages of the State Party. __________________________

text: CCPR/C/145/D/4294/2023Advance unedited versionDistr.: General26 March 2026Original: EnglishHuman Rights CommitteeDecision adopted by the Committee under the Optional Protocol, concerning communication No. 4294/2023*,**Submitted by:S.R.Alleged victim:The authorState Party:MoroccoDate of communication:17 January 2023Substantive issue:Extradition to USA1.The communication dated 17 January 2023 was submitted by S.R., a French national, born in 2001. At the time of the submission of the communication, the author was incarcerated in Morocco as part of extradition proceedings initiated by the Government of the United States. The author claimed that by extraditing him to the United States, the State Party would violate his rights under articles 7 and 14 3(b) of the Covenant. The author is represented by counsel. 2.On 25 January 2023, the author was extradited to the United States. On 31 January 2023, the Committee registered the communication and requested the State party to take interim measures to suspend the extradition, without knowing that it had already taken place. On 9 February 2023, the State Party informed the Committee that the extradition had preceded the Committee’s request for interim measures.3.On 13 October 2023 and 16 February 2024, the State party submitted observations on the admissibility and merits of the communication. On 9 April 2025, the State Party's observations were transmitted to the author's counsel for comments.4.On 16 June 2025, a reminder was sent to the author's counsel to submit his comments on the State Party's observations by 18 August 2025. Counsel was informed that, in the absence of a response, consideration of the communication could be terminated.5. In view of the fact that no response was received and that contact with the author was apparently lost, the Committee decided at its 145th session on 16 March 2026 to discontinue communication 4294/2023..
